1.  The present claim petition arises out of road accident in which one Gaurav Rawat suffered grievous injury. An application u/s 166(1) MV Act was accordingly filed by the claimant/applicant. 
Later, a Detailed Accident Report was also filed and the same was clubbed vide order dated 18.08.2018. 
2. Brief facts of the case are that on 31.12.2017 at about 6.50 PM, Petitioner was going to Sharma market from his working place Ratiya Marg Sangam Vihar as pillion rider with his friend on scooty bearing no. DL3S-BS-5298. When they reached TKD red light Surajkund, a dumper bearing no.
HR-38-N-8681 (hereinafter referred to as offending vehicle) hit the scooty from behind. As a result of the impact, victim fell and his right leg was run over by the offending truck. He was taken to Trauma Center AIIMS where he underwent treatment. The accident resulted in amputation of the right leg of the petitioner. 
3. An FIR 380/2017 was registered u/s 279,337 of IPC. Upon investigation, chargesheet u/s 279,338 IPC was filed before concerned criminal court against the driver of the offending vehicle(Respondent no.1) while present claim petition and DAR were filed before this Tribunal. 
4. Respondent no.1 is driver, Respondent no.2 is owner and Respondent no.3 is insurance company of the offending vehicle. 
MACT NO.369/18 Gaurav Rawat v. Kalyan Singh P.No. 2 Of 22 BK 5 . Respondent no.1 filed his reply denying negligence on his part. He claimed to be having a valid and effective driving licence and pleaded that the offending vehicle was duly insured on the date of accident. Respondent no.2 also filed his reply denying the involvement of offending vehicle in the accident. 
In its reply, respondent no.3 filed its reply pleaded that offending vehicle was being driven by its driver without licence and that the nature of injuries sustained by the petitioner could not be ascertained from the medical documents and report. 
6. Vide order dated 23.05.2019, following issues were framed. 
1. Whether the petitioner suffered injuries in a road traffic accident on 31.12.2017 due to rash and negligent driving of vehicle no.HR-38N-8681 being driven by R1, owned by R2 and insured with R3? OPP. 
2. Whether the petitioner is entitled to any compensation, if so, to what extent and from whom? 
OPP.
3. Relief.
7. Vide order dated 28.09.2022, interest of petitioner was closed from said date till conducting of evidence.

2 8. Petitioner examined himself as PW-1 and tendered his evidence by way of affidavit as Ex.PW-1/E.
He deposed that he was working as Manager with New Impression Shoes. On 31.12.2017 at around 6.50 pm, he was going to Sharma Market from his working place Ratiya Marg, Sangam Vihar. He was sitting behind his friend on scooty bearing no. DL-3S-BS-5298 and when they reached TKD red light, Surajkund, a dumper/offending vehicle bearing no.HR-38-N-8681 hit the MACT NO.369/18 Gaurav Rawat v. Kalyan Singh P.No. 3 Of 22 BK scooty from behind, due to which he fell down and sustained grievous injuries. Such offending vehicle was being driven rashly and negligently. He deposed that due to such accident, he lost his right leg and suffered permanent disability or 90%. He was working as Manager and earning Rs.15,450/- per month, but due to the accident and consequent disability, he lost his job. 
He relied upon salary slip for the month of July, 2017 to December 2017 as Mark-A, copy of Aadhar card as Mark-B, Disability certificate as Ex.PW-1/C, original medical bills as Ex.PW-1/D. Further evidence was recorded through learned Local Commissioner. PW-1 was duly cross - examined by Ld.
counsel for insurance company. 
Petitioner also examined Rashid Atiq was examined as PW-2 to prove his employment and income.
PW-2 tendered his evidence by way of affidavit as Ex.PW-2/X. He deposed that he was the proprietor of M/s. New Impression Shoes. He deposed that petitioner was working with him as Manager since 8-9 months and getting salary Rs.15,450/- p.m. He relied upon his Aadhar as Ex.PW-2/1 and salary slips as Ex.PW-2/2(colly). He was cross-examined by learned counsel for insurance company. 
No evidence has been led on behalf of the respondents. 
9. Final arguments in details were addressed on behalf of the claimant/injured and the insurance company. On the basis of pleadings of the parties, evidence adduced and arguments addressed,
issue wise findings are as under:
Whether the petitioner suffered injuries in a MACT NO.369/18 Gaurav Rawat v.
Kalyan Singh P.No. 4 Of 22 BK road traffic accident on 31.12.2017 due to rash and negligent driving of vehicle no.HR-38N-8681 being driven by R1, owned by R2 and insured with R3? OPP.
10. Before proceeding to decide the above issue, it is apposite to note that as a settled principle of law, proceedings under The Motor Vehicle Act are not considered akin to the proceedings in a civil suit and hence strict rules of evidence are not applicable. Reliance is placed upon decision in Bimla Devi & ors. vs. Himachal Road Transport Corporation & Ors. (2009) 13 SC 535, in Parmeshwari vs.
Amir Chand & Ors., 2011 (1) SCR 1096 and National Insurance Company Ltd. vs. Pushpa Rana,
2009 ACJ 287, wherein it has been held that the negligence has to be decided on the touchstone of preponderance of probabilities and a holistic view has to be taken.
11. In the instant case, petitioner Gaurav Rawat has testified the manner of accident. He has clearly and categorically stated that the offending truck had struck the vehicle on which he was travelling,
Gaurav Rawat vs Kalyan Singh on 13 December, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/59462702/
3 from behind. During cross-examination as PW-1 he has testified that his scooty was at a speed of around 20-30 Km./h. This averment has not been refuted by any suggestion or cross question by any of the respondents. No suggestion denying the occurrence of the accident or involvement of the offending vehicle has been put to PW-1. It is evident from the material on record that the vehicle on which the petitioner was a pillion rider was hit by the offending truck from behind. No defence has been raised by the driver of the offending truck as to negligent driving on the part of the vehicle on which petitioner was a pillion rider. 
Further, after investigating even the police has filed a MACT NO.369/18 Gaurav Rawat v. Kalyan Singh P.No. 5 Of 22 BK chargesheet against Respondent no.1 which shows that the accident was reported without any inordinate delay. The site plan, mechanical inspection report and photographs of the offending vehicle are suggestive of negligence on the part of the driver of the offending vehicle. In National Insurance Co. vs. Pushpa Rana 2009 ACJ 287 Delhi, it was laid down that completion of investigation and filing of charge sheet are sufficient proof of negligence of the driver of the offending vehicle. 
A defence has been raised by insurance company in the cross-examination of PW-1 by suggesting that the petitioner contributed to the accident in as much as neither the driver of the scooty nor the petitioner were wearing any helmet. This suggestion has not been denied. It has also been suggested to PW-1 that he and the driver of the scooty were intoxicated at the time of accident. This suggestion has been denied by PW-1. Further, there is nothing in the MLC or discharge summary or any other medical document to show that the petitioner or the driver of the scooty were under influence of alcohol. Suggestion qua driving licence of petitioner has also been put in the cross- examination. 
In the considered opinion of the court, mere not wearing of helmet did not contribute to the occurrence of the accident, which is proved to have been caused due to negligence on the part of respondent no.1. Similarly, the plea that the driver of the motorbike on which petitioner was riding,
did not have a valid driving licence is not a fact that contributed to the negligence on the part of the petitioner. Whether or not petitioner, being simplicitor a pillion rider, had a driving licence is immaterial to MACT NO.369/18 Gaurav Rawat v. Kalyan Singh P.No. 6 Of 22 BK the case as he was not the one who was driving the scooty. 
12. In totality of circumstances, this Tribunal is of the opinion that the petitioner has been able to prove on the scales of preponement of probabilities that the accident in question took place due to rash and negligent driving of the offending vehicle by its driver/respondent no.1 on the date and time of accident. Accordingly, issue no.1 is decided in favour of petitioner and against the respondents. 
Issue no. 2 Whether the petitioner is entitled to any compensation, if so, to what extent and from whom? OPP. 
13. Insurance company had raised its defence in written statement that driver of offending vehicle was not possessing valid driving licence but it has not led any evidence in this regard. Further, there is nothing in the FIR or the chargesheet to show that the driver of the offending vehicle was also Gaurav Rawat vs Kalyan Singh on 13 December, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/59462702/
4 charged for driving without a valid licence. As such, effectively, there is no statutory defence in the case and accordingly, insurance company is liable to compensate the petitioner. 
14. As regards the quantum of compensation, this court is governed by the law laid down by Hon'le Supreme Court in Raj Kumar Vs. Ajay Kumar & Anr. (2011) 1 Supreme Court cases 343, Sarla Verma & Ors. v. Delhi Transport Corporation & Ors. (2003) 6SCC 121 and National Insurance Company Limited v. Pranay Sethi & Ors.(2017) 16 SCC 680. The gist of the law is that the object of awarding damages is to make good the loss suffered as a result of wrong done as far as money can do so, in a MACT NO.369/18 Gaurav Rawat v. Kalyan Singh P.No. 7 Of 22 BK fair, reasonable and equitable manner. The court or the Tribunal shall have to assess the damages objectively and exclude from consideration any speculation or fancy, though some conjecture with reference to the nature of disability and its consequences, is inevitable. A person is not only to be compensated for the physical injury, but also for the loss which he suffered as a result of such injury. This means that he is to be compensated for his inability to lead a full life, his inability to enjoy those normal amenities which he would have enjoyed but for the injuries, and his inability to earn as much as he used to earn or could have earned. 
15. Further it can be noted that the heads under which compensation is awarded in personal injury cases are the following:
Pecuniary damages (Special damages)
(i) Expenses relating to treatment, hospitalisation, medicines, transportation,
nourishing food, and miscellaneous expenditure.
(ii) Loss of earnings (and other gains) which the injured would have made had he not been injured, comprising:
(a) Loss of earning during the period of treatment;
(b) Loss of future earnings on account of permanent disability. 
(iii) Future medical expenses. 
Non-pecuniary damages (General damages) 
(iv) Damages for pain, suffering and trauma as a consequence of the injuries. 
(v) Loss of amenities (and/or loss of prospects of MACT NO.369/18 Gaurav Rawat v.
Kalyan Singh P.No. 8 Of 22 BK marriage). 
(vi) Loss of expectation of life (shortening of normal longevity). 
Gaurav Rawat vs Kalyan Singh on 13 December, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/59462702/
5 15.1. In routine personal injury cases, compensation will be awarded only under heads (i), (ii) (a)
and (iv). 15.2. It is only in serious cases of injury, where there is specific medical evidence corroborating the evidence of the claimant, that compensation will be granted under any of the heads (ii)(b), (iii),
(v) and (vi) relating to loss of future earnings on account of permanent disability, future medical expenses, loss of amenities (and/or loss of prospects of marriage) and loss of expectation of life.
15.3. Assessment of pecuniary damages under Item (i) and under Item (ii) (a) do not pose much difficulty as they involve reimbursement of actuals and are easily ascertainable from the evidence.
15.4. Award under the head of future medical expenses--Item (iii)--depends upon specific medical evidence regarding need for further treatment and cost thereof. 
15.5. Assessment of non-pecuniary damages--Items (iv), (v) and (vi)--involves determination of l u m p s u m a m o u n t s w i t h r e f e r e n c e t o c i r c u m s t a n c e s s u c h a s a g e , n a t u r e o f injury/deprivation/disability suffered by the claimant and the effect thereof on the future life of the claimant. Decisions of Hon'ble Supreme Court and Hon'ble High Courts contain necessary guidelines for award under these heads, if necessary. 15.6. Observation of Hon'ble Supreme Court in Rajkumar v. Ajay Kumar & Anr. is quoted hereunder:
MACT NO.369/18 Gaurav Rawat v. Kalyan Singh P.No. 9 Of 22 BK "10.
Ascertainment of the effect of the permanent disability on the actual earning capacity involves three steps. The Tribunal has to first ascertain what activities the claimant could carry on in spite of the permanent disability and what he could not do as a result of the permanent ability (this is also relevant for awarding compensation under the head of loss of amenities of life). The second step is to ascertain his avocation,
profession and nature of work before the accident, as also his age. The third step is to find out whether (i) the claimant is totally disabled from earning any kind of livelihood, or (ii) whether in spite of the permanent disability, the claimant could still effectively carry on the activities and functions, which he was earlier carrying on, or (iii) whether he was prevented or restricted from discharging his previous activities and functions, but could carry on some other or lesser scale of activities and functions so that he continues to earn or can continue to earn his livelihood. For example, if the left hand of a claimant is amputated, the permanent physical or functional disablement may be assessed around 60%. If the claimant was a driver or a carpenter, the actual loss of earning capacity may virtually be hundred percent, if he is neither able to drive or do carpentry. On the other hand, if the claimant was a clerk in government service, the loss of his left hand may not result in loss of employment and he may still be continued as a clerk as he could perform his clerical functions;
and in that event the loss of earning capacity will not be 100% as in the case of a driver or carpenter, nor 60% which is the actual physical disability, but far less. In fact, there may not be any need to award any compensation under the head of `loss of Gaurav Rawat vs Kalyan Singh on 13 December, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/59462702/
6 future earnings', if the claimant continues in government service, though he may be awarded compensation under the head of loss of amenities as a consequence of losing his hand. Sometimes the injured claimant may be continued in service, but may not found suitable for discharging the duties attached to the post or job which he was earlier holding, on account of his disability, and may therefore be shifted to some other suitable but lesser post with lesser emoluments, in which case there should be a limited award under the head of loss of future earning capacity, taking note of the reduced earning capacity. It may be noted that when compensation is awarded by treating the loss of future earning capacity as 100% (or even anything more than 50%), the need to award compensation MACT NO.369/18 Gaurav Rawat v. Kalyan Singh P.No. 10 Of 22 BK separately under the head of loss of amenities or loss of expectation of life may disappear and as a result, only a token or nominal amount may have to be awarded under the head of loss of amenities or loss of expectation of life, as otherwise there may be a duplication in the award of compensation.
Pecuniary /Special Damages (i) Loss of earnings.
Actual loss of earning:
16. As regards loss of income, petitioner has claimed to be working as Manager in M/s. New Impression Shoes and earning Rs.15,450/- p.m. The income as well as the employment of the petitioner has been disputed by the insurance company. Petitioner has examined one Rashid Atiq as PW-2 to prove that such PW-2 was employer of PW-1. PW-2 has testified to be proprietor of New Impression Shoes and claimed that the petitioner/PW-1 was working a Manager in his company since 8- 9 months @ monthly salary of Rs.15,450/-. During cross- examination, PW-2 has failed to produce any document to show that he is proprietor of any such company or firm. No record of the company or ledger account has been filed. Even the salary slips filed on record are neither attested nor certified with any signatures of the employer or stamp of the company. Such salary slip does not even mention the designation or any other detail of the employee/petitioner. It is doubtful that while the employer as allegedly issuing salary slips to the petitioner, he was paying salary to the petitioner in cash. Further, during his cross- examination, PW-2 has stated that that the petitioner was on duty in his shop on the date of accident i.e. 31.12.2017 from 9.30 AM to 8.30 PM. This fact is contradictory to the averment that the MACT NO.369/18 Gaurav Rawat v. Kalyan Singh P.No. 11 Of 22 BK accident took place at 6.50 PM, when the petitioner would have been working in the shop. As such, PW-2 is not a reliable witness and the alleged salary slip filed by him cannot be taken as a proof of employment or income/salary of the petitioner. Further, petitioner has claimed himself to be 10th passed, however, has not filed any proof of his educational qualification. He is thus assumed to be an unskilled labour working at minimum wages prevalent in Delhi at the time of accident. The minimum wages of an unskilled labour in Delhi as on 31.12.2017 were Rs.13,584/-. 
As per record, petitioner was referred to Batra hospital on 31.12.2017 where he was diagnosed with Degloving injury with bones and muscles and vasculetase exposed on the right thigh. He was Gaurav Rawat vs Kalyan Singh on 13 December, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/59462702/
7 admitted to Jai Prakash Narain, Apex AIIMS on 04.01.2018 and discharged on 05.01.2018. As he was diagnosed with soft tissue injury and FUC of hip disarticulation complaining of bleed from SX site. It is a matter of record that the petitioner not only suffered grievous injuries but also amputation of his right leg due to the accident. He has also underwent surgery in relation to the injuries. Considering the nature of injury and the part of the body amputated, it is assumed that the petitioner may have been incapacitated from working for at least six month. 
As such, petitioner is assumed to have suffered actual loss of earning to the tune of Rs.13,584X6=81,504/-. Accordingly, petitioner is entitled to compensation towards loss of income as Rs.81,504/-.
MACT NO.369/18 Gaurav Rawat v. Kalyan Singh P.No. 12 Of 22 BK Loss of future income/earnings:
17. In the present case, petitioner has relied upon disability certificate issued from Pt.
Madan Mohan Malviya hospital, noticing permanent disability of 90% in relation to right lower limb. Considering the age and nature of employment of the petitioner, the functional disability of the petitioner is taken as same as his permanent disability i.e.
80%.
Since the date of birth of the petitioner as per his Aadhar card is 01.01.1995, his age at the time of accident on 31.12.2017 would have been 22 years. As such, for purpose of calculating loss of future income, a multiplier of 18 (petitioner aged about 22 years), as per Sarla Verma judgment, would be applicable in the case and 40% would be added as future prospect as Pranay Sethi judgment. Hence,
compensation towards loss of future income is assessed to Rs.13,584/-(monthly income)X18(multiplier)+40% of total income(as future prospect)=Rs.3,42,317/-. 80% of this amount would be Rs.2,73,854/-. Hence so awarded. 
(ii) Future Medical Expenses:
18. Since there is amputation of right leg of the petitioner caused due to injury in the accident. However, no document has been placed regarding implantation of artificial limb. As such, on approximation basis, a sum of Rs.5,00,000/- is granted towards future medical expenses(inclusive of implantation of artificial limb and its time to time repair). 
(iii) Expenses relating to treatment:
19. Petitioner has relied upon discharge slip and original medical bills as Ex.PW-1/D.
Medical bills are amounting to Rs.1,15,034/- and are accordingly awarded towards medical MACT NO.369/18 Gaurav Rawat v. Kalyan Singh P.No. 13 Of 22 BK expenses. 
Apart from expenditure on treatment, a sum of Rs.25,000/- under each head i.e. conveyance &
special diet and Rs.60,000/- on account of cost of nursing/ attendant is granted to the petitioner.

27. At this stage, it is relevant to the refer to the judgment of A. V. Padma & Ors. Vs.,
R. Venugopal & Ors. (2012) 3 Supreme Court Cases 378:
" ......In the case of Susamma Thomas (supra), this Court issued certain guidelines in order to "safeguard the feed from being frittered away by the beneficiaries due to ignorance, illiteracy and susceptibility to exploitation". 
Even as per the guidelines issued by this Court Court, long term fixed deposit of amount of compensation is mandatory only in the case of minors, illiterate claimants and widows. In the case of illiterate claimants, the Tribunal is allowed to consider the request for lumpsum payment for effecting purchase of any movable property such as agricultural implements, rickshaws etc. to earn a living. However, in such cases, the Tribunal shall make sure that the amount is actually spent for the purpose and the demand is not a ruse to withdraw money. In the case of semi-illiterate claimants,
the Tribunal should ordinarily invest the amount of compensation in long term fixed deposit. But if the Tribunal is satisfied for reasons to be stated in writing that the whole or part of the amount is required for expanding an existing business or for purchasing some property for earning a livelihood, the Tribunal can release the whole or part of the amount of compensation to the claimant provided the Tribunal will ensure that the amount is invested for the purpose for which it is demanded and paid. In the case of literate persons, it is not mandatory to invest the amount of compensation in long term fixed deposit.

11 The expression used in guideline No. (iv) issued by this Court is that in the case of literate persons also the Tribunal may resort to the procedure indicated in guideline No. (i), whereas in the guideline Nos. MACT NO.369/18 Gaurav Rawat v. Kalyan Singh P.No. 18 Of 22 BK (i), (ii), (iii) and (v), the expression used is that the Tribunal should. Moreover, in the case of literate persons, the Tribunal may resort to the procedure indicated in guideline No. (i) only if, having regard to the age, fiscal background and strata of the society to which the claimant belongs and such other considerations, the Tribunal thinks that in the larger interest of the claimant and with a view to ensure the safety of the compensation awarded, it is necessary to invest the amount of compensation in long term fixed deposit.
Thus, sufficient discretion has been given to the Tribunal not to insist on investment of the compensation amount in long term fixed deposit and to release even the whole amount in the case of literate persons. However, the Tribunals are often taking a very rigid stand and are mechanically ordering in almost all cases that the amount of compensation shall be invested in long term fixed deposit. They are taking such a rigid and mechanical approach without understanding and appreciating the distinction drawn by this Court in the case of minors, illiterate claimants and widows and in the case of semiliterate and literate persons. It needs to be clarified that the above guidelines were issued by this Court only to safeguard the interests of the claimants, particularly the minors, illiterates and others whose amounts are sought to be withdrawn on some fictitious grounds. The guidelines were not to be understood to mean that the Tribunals were to take a rigid stand while considering an application seeking release of the money.
